title: The peace
hook: peace be with you, and with your spirit: a handshake, hug or bow

segments.voice: Yesterday, the creed said together, a whole room in one voice. Your line was we believe. What did you say alongside other people, and what did the room sound like? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Hand out, then a tiny pause. Is this a handshake person, a hug person, or a nod-from-across-the-aisle person? In the middle of the service, everything stops for a minute and strangers turn to greet each other. A small boy shakes every hand within reach, twice. Two people who snapped at each other in the parking lot meet eyes and have to decide something. A woman in the front bows with her palms together. And the same words go back and forth across the pews: "Peace be with you." "And with your spirit." Today: the peace.

The peace looks like a social break. In the rite it's something more: the church making peace with itself before it goes any further. It has four roots worth knowing. First, a locked room. In John's Gospel, on the evening of the resurrection, the disciples are behind shut doors, afraid. Jesus comes and stands among them, and his first words are not a complaint. In the King James Bible: "Peace be unto you." A couple of verses later, he says it again. Christians who pass the peace are passing on his greeting. Second, the early letters. Near the end of his letter to the church in Rome, Paul writes a line that would startle some congregations now: "Salute one another with an holy kiss." Some churches still call this moment the kiss of peace. In the Orthodox liturgy it comes just before the creed, with a call to love one another so that the church can confess its faith with one mind. Third, the gift. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says that if you bring your gift to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Some churches place the peace just before the gifts come forward, with that verse in mind. In the Catholic Mass the sign of peace comes later, just before communion. Same gesture, a different place in the service, a meaning in each. Fourth, the hands. A handshake in one country, a bow in another, a hug in a small church where everyone knows everyone. The form bends. The words stay.
screen: `A LOCKED ROOM: PEACE BE UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet someone with peace. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind. It can be someone you love. It can be someone you're at odds with right now, the parking-lot person in your life. Picture their face clearly, and hold it for a moment without arguing with it. Then, silently, wish them peace. If you pray, you can say the risen Jesus's words over them: peace be unto you. If you don't, simply wish them well and mean it, even a little. If a second face shows up, greet that one too. The bell holds the time.
The peace. The moment in a service when people greet one another with Jesus's words, peace be with you, before going on together.
Your line: peace be with you. Today, greet one person as if the greeting meant something: eyes up, a real wish for their good. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and some other churches, the congregation exchanges a sign of peace during the service with a handshake, embrace or bow, saying "peace be with you"; where it falls in the service differs from church to church.

original.note: Greek: peace, the word in Jesus's greeting to the disciples in John 20:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: a minute to say hi to the people next to you.
what it means: a rite of reconciliation, passing on the greeting the risen Jesus gave his frightened friends.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 5 puts reconciliation before the offering, and some churches place the peace just before the gifts come forward with that in mind.

notes: Response 'And with your spirit' is the current Catholic English wording; some churches say 'And also with you'. Only one given in the hook; confirm.

Orthodox placement: the kiss of peace with 'Let us love one another, that with one mind we may confess' before the Creed is paraphrased; confirm, and confirm that in many parishes it is exchanged mainly among clergy.
Catholic placement (sign of peace after the Lord's Prayer, before communion) and 'some churches' placing it before the offertory (e.g. Anglican, Lutheran) stated without numbers; confirm.
'Some churches still call this moment the kiss of peace' — confirm.
John 20:19 'for fear of the Jews' deliberately not quoted; the disciples are described as 'afraid'.
